facts.statement: Aggressive driving involves an intentional driving action or moving traffic violation that endangers people or property.
Speeding, tailgating and unsafe lane changes are examples associated with aggressive driving.
Ignoring traffic controls or signaling improperly can be part of aggressive driving.
Threatening another driver with a weapon, making hostile gestures or chasing a vehicle to cause harm are examples associated with aggressive driving.
To avoid aggressive driving, relax and concentrate on the driving task.
Use the posted speed limit and plan a realistic travel time to reduce aggressive driving.
Courteous and forgiving behavior helps prevent aggressive driving.
Leave the area if possible and report serious aggressive behavior.
Alcohol or other impairing drugs increase collision risk even in small amounts.
People younger than 21 may not purchase, possess or drink alcoholic beverages.
Alcohol and impairing drugs reduce perception, emergency response and vehicle-control ability.
Alcohol and impairing drugs interfere with the brain functions used for judgment.
Alcohol and some drugs can blur sight, delay focusing or cause double vision.
Alcohol and impairing drugs reduce the ability to judge distance, speed and other vehicles' motion.
Increasing impairment can lead to lane wandering, crossing the center line or leaving the road.
The handbook states that vision is affected at a BAC of.02.
Alcohol and impairing drugs can reduce the ability to tell road-sign and signal colors apart.
Alcohol and impairing drugs slow information processing and responses to driving tasks.
Alcohol and impairing drugs can cause drowsiness and reduce awareness of surroundings.
Do not let a friend or relative drive after drinking.
For a friend or relative who has been drinking, the handbook suggests taking away their keys.
Arrange a driver who has not been drinking for a friend or relative who has consumed alcohol.
Calling a taxi is an alternative to letting a friend or relative drive after drinking.
Having a friend or relative stay overnight is an alternative to letting them drive after drinking.
Coffee does not remove alcohol or other drugs from circulation.
Fresh air does not remove alcohol or other drugs from circulation.
A cold shower does not remove alcohol or other drugs from circulation.
Eating does not remove alcohol or other drugs from circulation.
The handbook identifies passage of time as the only medically proven way to remove alcohol or drug combinations from circulation.
Even a first alcoholic drink can impair the ability to drive.
The safest advice in the handbook is to avoid driving after consuming alcohol or impairing drugs.
A BAC of.08 or greater violates the alcohol-driving law described in the handbook.
For a BAC of.08 or higher, the handbook describes a possible 30-day suspension and criminal penalties.
Kansas drivers below 21 can be arrested for alcohol impairment at a BAC of.02 percent.
BAC expresses the alcohol level in the body as a percentage of blood.
A driver can still be impaired and convicted of impaired driving below a BAC of.08.
An alcohol-concentration test usually uses breath, blood or urine to measure alcohol in the body.
Kansas implied consent treats obtaining a license as agreement to a lawfully requested alcohol test by a police officer when impaired driving is suspected.
The handbook says refusing a lawfully requested police alcohol test when impaired driving is suspected can lead to losing a license for one year.
For a first alcohol-driving conviction, the handbook describes a possible fine of 750 to 1000 dollars plus court costs.
For a first alcohol-driving conviction, the handbook describes a possible sentence of at least 48 hours in jail or 100 hours of community service.
The handbook says a first alcohol-driving conviction results in license suspension.
The handbook requires driving with an ignition-interlock device after a first alcohol-driving conviction.
Second and later alcohol-driving convictions carry more severe penalties under the handbook.
Prescription and nonprescription drugs can impair driving as much as or more than alcohol.
Some headache, cold, allergy and calming medicines can cause drowsiness that affects driving.
Stimulant and diet pills may cause dizziness, nervousness, concentration trouble or vision problems.
Read nonprescription drug warnings before taking the product.
Ask a doctor or pharmacist about driving effects when a drug's safety is unclear.
Prescription drugs may impair reflexes, judgment, sight and alertness.
Antidepressants, pain medicines, sleep aids and sedatives may affect safe driving.
Read prescription and package warnings about a medicine's effects before taking it.
Illegal drugs can impair reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness.
The handbook reports that marijuana users make more driving mistakes and have more trouble adjusting to glare than other drivers.
For a first drug-impaired-driving conviction, the handbook lists a fine from 750 to 1000 dollars plus court costs.
For a first drug-impaired-driving conviction, the handbook lists at least 48 jail hours or 100 community-service hours.
The handbook describes license suspension after a first drug-impaired-driving conviction.
Later drug-impaired-driving convictions carry more severe penalties.
Do not combine drinking alcohol with other drugs.
Combining alcohol and drugs can magnify impairment and cause serious illness or death.
Driving experience does not make alcohol-impaired or drug-impaired driving safe.
Even a cold, stiff neck, cough or sore leg can affect driving.
If illness makes you unwell, ask someone else to drive.
Ask a doctor about a health condition that may prevent safe driving.
Strong emotions can disrupt thinking, attention and information processing while driving.
Strong worry, excitement, fear, anger or depression may prevent safe driving.
If angry or excited, stay off the road until you calm down.
A short walk or nap can help an angry or excited person settle before driving.
When worried or upset, keep attention on driving rather than the upsetting issue.
Some drivers find radio listening helpful when worried or upset, provided it does not distract them from safe driving.
An impatient driver should allow extra trip time and leave earlier.
Do not dart through traffic or drive faster than the traffic flow because of impatience.
Having another person drive is an option when emotions interfere with safe driving.
According to the handbook, every state has zero-tolerance or similar alcohol laws for drivers younger than 21.
Judgment draws on a person's experience and knowledge when facing a new problem.
In the handbook, being sober means having no alcohol or other impairing drugs in circulation.
Under the Kansas implied-consent rule described in the handbook, a driver suspected of impaired driving must take a BAC test when a police officer lawfully requests it.
The handbook prohibits purchasing, possessing or consuming illegal drugs.
The handbook reports more traffic-violation arrests among marijuana users than other drivers.
The handbook says a first drug-impaired-driving conviction may also bring other criminal penalties.
Emotions can increase risk-taking while driving.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Aggressive driving intentionally uses a driving action or traffic violation to endanger people or property.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Aggressive driving involves an intentional driving action or moving traffic violation that endangers people or property.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Intentionally acts so as to endanger changes the definition from intent to perform the action to purpose of endangering.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Threats, hostile gestures and chasing another vehicle to cause harm are aggressive behaviors.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Threatening another driver with a weapon, making hostile gestures or chasing a vehicle to cause harm are examples associated with aggressive driving.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Generic threats omit the source's weapon qualification.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Taking a drinking person's keys is one way the handbook suggests preventing an impaired trip.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: For a friend or relative who has been drinking, the handbook suggests taking away their keys.
changed_existing_facts.issue: A drinking person broadens the actor beyond the source's friend or relative.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Arrange a driver who has not been drinking for someone who consumed alcohol.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Arrange a driver who has not been drinking for a friend or relative who has consumed alcohol.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Someone drops the stated friend-or-relative context.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: A taxi is an alternative to letting a drinking person drive.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Calling a taxi is an alternative to letting a friend or relative drive after drinking.
changed_existing_facts.issue: A drinking person drops the stated friend-or-relative context.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: An overnight stay is an alternative to driving after drinking.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Having a friend or relative stay overnight is an alternative to letting them drive after drinking.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The standalone overnight suggestion omits who it concerns.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook identifies time as the medically established way for alcohol or drug combinations to leave circulation.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: The handbook identifies passage of time as the only medically proven way to remove alcohol or drug combinations from circulation.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Medically established way does not explicitly preserve only medically proven method.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: BAC expresses the proportion of alcohol relative to the amount of blood in the body.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: BAC expresses the alcohol level in the body as a percentage of blood.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Proportion omits the source's percentage scale, which matters when interpreting the small numeric BAC values.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Kansas implied consent treats obtaining a license as agreement to a lawfully requested alcohol test when impaired driving is suspected.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Kansas implied consent treats obtaining a license as agreement to a lawfully requested alcohol test by a police officer when impaired driving is suspected.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The police-officer actor is absent from the standalone implied-consent description.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook states that refusing an alcohol test can result in losing a license for one year.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: The handbook says refusing a lawfully requested police alcohol test when impaired driving is suspected can lead to losing a license for one year.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Any alcohol-test refusal is broader than refusal of the lawfully requested police test described.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: For a first alcohol conviction, the handbook lists a fine from 750 to 1000 dollars plus court costs.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: For a first alcohol-driving conviction, the handbook describes a possible fine of 750 to 1000 dollars plus court costs.
changed_existing_facts.issue: First alcohol conviction is not self-contained about the driving-offense context.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: For a first alcohol conviction, the handbook lists at least 48 jail hours or 100 community-service hours.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: For a first alcohol-driving conviction, the handbook describes a possible sentence of at least 48 hours in jail or 100 hours of community service.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The driving-offense context is absent from the standalone penalty statement.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: A first alcohol conviction carries license suspension under the handbook's description.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: The handbook says a first alcohol-driving conviction results in license suspension.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The driving-offense context is absent from the standalone suspension statement.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook requires an ignition-interlock device after a first alcohol conviction.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: The handbook requires driving with an ignition-interlock device after a first alcohol-driving conviction.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The driving-offense context is omitted, and the source requires using the interlock when driving rather than an unqualified device-possession duty.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Second and later alcohol convictions carry more severe penalties.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Second and later alcohol-driving convictions carry more severe penalties under the handbook.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Generic alcohol convictions broaden the source's driving-offense context.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Some headache, cold, allergy and calming medicines cause drowsiness that affects driving.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Some headache, cold, allergy and calming medicines can cause drowsiness that affects driving.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Cause drowsiness removes the source's can qualification.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook associates marijuana use with more mistakes and trouble adapting to glare.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: The handbook reports that marijuana users make more driving mistakes and have more trouble adjusting to glare than other drivers.
changed_existing_facts.issue: More mistakes and glare difficulty lacks the source's comparison with other drivers.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: Being very worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed may prevent safe driving.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Strong worry, excitement, fear, anger or depression may prevent safe driving.
changed_existing_facts.issue: The strength qualifier is ambiguous across the standalone list; make the excessive-intensity condition explicit for all listed emotions.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook allows listening to the radio as a calming aid only when it does not distract from driving.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Some drivers find radio listening helpful when worried or upset, provided it does not distract them from safe driving.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Allows as a calming aid broadens a qualified observation about some drivers into a general permission.

unverifiable_dispositions.original_statement: New drivers learning complex skills are especially affected by alcohol and impairing drugs.

debts.text: Withheld assertion sec03-R12: New drivers learning complex skills are especially affected by alcohol and impairing drugs. Reason: The cited page contains the predicate but not the new-driver subject. The comparison is supported only by reading a sentence across two pages; it cannot satisfy the one-page fact rule as currently cited. The original meaning, quantity and source page are retained here as unresolved debt; it is not a learner fact.

The handbook attributes more driving mistakes, glare-adjustment difficulty and traffic-violation arrests among marijuana users than other drivers to studies that are unnamed and undated on the cited page. The attributed handbook statements are retained, while identification and date of the underlying research remain explicit provenance debt; no present external research validity is asserted.
